speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head P of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Home Team plays an important role in keeping Singapore safe from terror threats.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our TransCom officers conduct high-visibility patrols at bus interchanges and Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) stations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Not just called upon in day-to-day operations to keep Singaporeans safe, the Home Team also does an excellent job during times of heightened security risks, such as hosting of key international meetings.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In 2018, we hosted the Trump-Kim summit and the 33rd Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In 2019, we hosted the signing of the Singapore Convention on Mediation which required large-scale operations to protect the many dignitaries from different countries and to maintain law and order during the large-scale event.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The changing global landscape of crime and crime-related activities has an impact on Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Through the Internet, crime is no longer confined to the physical territorial boundaries of a country and much harm can be done by a person even without stepping onto our shores.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Home Team has proven itself as a formidable force, having to deal with the global threat of terrorism and its implications on Singapore; increasing recreational drug use in the region and the world; and having to deal with ensuring law and order for multiple high-key international events hosted in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There is also the threat of foreign interference in our domestic politics.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There is also the threat which fake news can pose to ongoing security operations conducted by the Home Team.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In fact, when fake news is bandied about on WhatsApp during very important security operations by the Home Team, it does impact the operational ability of that exercise and that operation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This list of threats stands to get longer as the world becomes smaller.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Home Team can remain effective and operational notwithstanding these pressures.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, our Home Team can leverage science and technology, intelligence gathering, cooperation with other enforcement agencies, predicting future threats early and recruiting dedicated officers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would the Minister elaborate on how the Home Team is leveraging each of these aspects to ensure it continues to safeguard Singapore from new and emerging threats in addition to its important everyday functions of maintaining law and order?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Mr Chairman, the Singapore Police Force (SPF) 200 Exhibition "Frontier Town to Safest City" captured the essence of SPF's remarkable journey from a 12-man team to a formidable and effective force of 15,000 today.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: As Minister Shanmugam said at the launch of the exhibition, over the years, SPF has had to deal with the relevant threats of the times – opium, gambling, secret societies, prostitution, conflicts and unrest among different groups.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The security landscape has changed in those 200 years, but the Police Force’s values and mission remain the same – integrity in maintaining law and order.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It is only right that in the course of this year’s Committee of Supply (COS) debate that we use the opportunity to thank the dedicated officers of our SPF for their professionalism and readiness to protect law and order in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Looking ahead, in today’s fast-changing security landscape, would the Minister share how the Home Team would transform to ensure that it continues its relevance, operational-readiness and efficiency?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Recently, we have seen a proliferation of large-scale chaos and riots in other countries.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: These have caused immense damage and disruption to essential services in those societies.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: How can our Home Team guard Singapore and its essential services against such dangerous security risks?

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mr Chairman, growing up in the 1970s and 1980s, the Police were some sort of a mystic, so there is a mysterious part to the Police Force.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When I was growing up in a Teochew kampung, my parents always say "mata liak" or Police will catch you, if you are not doing the right things.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But that transformed later on in school when we went for a road safety campaign, and we saw the policemen teaching us how to obey the safety rules, traffic rules and they were extremely friendly.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, it changed my perception that the engagement between the public and the Police was friendly, and you can have a lot of confidence and trust in them.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, that is no mean feat because as I became a Member of Parliament, and I dealt with the Sengkang Neighbourhood Police Post, every single one of the policemen, when they engage the public, that friendliness and confidence are there and you can tell that the public trust them, so much so that even the smallest of things they would send a complaint or report to the policeman.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: That makes them really, really "see beh boh eng", very busy.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we made progress, I realised it is more and more difficult to maintain that public trust for our policemen, especially when there is social media – the social media, with its fake news or real news or even pictures.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A picture, although it speaks a thousand words, but then again, if it is the wrong caption, then it would actually affect the trust and confidence in the policemen.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, in this day and age, with the world changing really fast, and with social media and information overload, how is SPF or how is the Ministry going to maintain that public trust and confidence in our Police Force?

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Moving forward, what are the measures and also plans that they will Implement and execute in order to uphold that trust?

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Because with that trust, then our enforcement officers can do their work and we can still continue to be ranked No 1 in the Global Order Index.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: With new challenges emerging, their work gets tougher.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I am heartened that the Home Team has transformed its operations throughout the years.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: With the celebration of SPF's 200th Anniversary this year, can the Minister share how does our Home Team remain relevant to meet our evolving security needs?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, the recent Hong Kong protests had shown how quickly mass gatherings can degenerate into chaos, resulting in injuries and even deaths and damage to properties.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While this is a very different situation from Hong Kong, it shows that unexpected events can lead to people gathering and the Home Team must always be on the ready to ensure order.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Ministry share what lessons we have learnt from the Hong Kong protests and how would the Home Team prevent similar incidents from happening in Singapore?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, transnational families form a significant proportion of our population today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Such families often live with tremendous uncertainty because the foreign spouse must continuously apply for the right to stay in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA) does not publicly disclose the exact criteria for granting or renewing a visit pass.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Foreign spouses are placed in a vulnerable position within their marriage because of this uncertainty.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Community organisations which work with abuse survivors or migrants have seen many cases of the citizen spouse threatening to cancel their pass as a way to abuse their foreign wives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Transnational families, particularly lower-income ones, also have limited housing options.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Citizens can purchase Housing and Development Board (HDB) flats but they are treated as singles for housing grants and foreign spouses cannot be co-owners.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In cases of divorce or widowhood, the foreign spouse faces even more uncertainty.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The Government has said it will help facilitate a renewable Long-Term Visit Pass (LTVP), as long as they have custody over young Singaporean children.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is very welcome but not a guarantee.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The foreign spouse also has no right to occupy or inherit an HDB flat, causing great anxiety over housing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Government allow citizens married to LTVP+ holders to qualify as a family for the Public Rental Scheme?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Government provide greater support and protection to these vulnerable families by granting the LTVP+ to all foreign spouses of citizens?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Government consider creating a clear, timed pathway for these foreign spouses to obtain Permanent Residence status?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Chairman, leveraging science and technology will aid our Home Team officers in ensuring we have the capability to deter, fend off and overcome new threats.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Technology has the benefit of allowing officers to perform critical roles with greater time and focus.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Would the Minister please provide an update on how the Home Team Science and Technology Agency (HTX) will enhance our Home Team’s fight against new and emerging threats?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How will the work of HTX help in operational effectiveness of the Home Team?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Having the right talent and skills is critical for the success of HTC.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Has HTX been successful in attracting the right talent it requires for the scale and scope of its ambitious mandate?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Could the Minister also share the profile of the HTX team?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: One of HTX's people strategy is to enable integration across the Home Team to bring together capabilities, knowledge and resources from different Home Team departments.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How has HTX brought together the capabilities across the different Home Team departments?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Does HTX have the right talents who are able to translate security operational requirements into technology solutions and what are some of these solutions?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As HTX is a new organisation, what are the early challenges it is facing?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What are the risks involved in the use of technology in the Home Team's operations and how is the Home Team addressing these risks?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Its work in security technologies and research as well as the prevention, response and recovery from cyberattacks requires interagency coordination and industry partnerships.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How is the Home Team developing HTX's interagency cooperation and industry collaborations?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In keeping Singapore safe and secure, the Home Team has to tackle an increasing complex security environment and, at most times, the problem to be solved is not always defined or predictable.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Operationally, officers have to deal with vast information, complex and fast-evolving situations and manage risks.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In such an environment, could the Minister share the Home Team’s approach to skills and capability building of its officers?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How does the Home Team track the effectiveness of these capability development programmes?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the pace of change, how do the Home Team’s capability development programmes enable continual learning?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Technology continues to play an increasing role in homeland security, and the environment that officers have to deal with range from the physical to cyber.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How does the Home Team ensure that its officers are adequately prepared and equipped to adapt and leverage new technologies and solutions to effectively deploy them in their operations?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The Home Team must now operate within the confines of many unknowns and some of these crimes and threats cut across continents and boundaries, both physically and virtually.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In the same vein, the workforce profile in Singapore is changing rapidly and, with an extremely tight labour market, an ageing workforce and imminent negative employment growth in a few years’ time, against this backdrop, how will the Home Team leverage technology to mitigate emerging threats and manpower constraints?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As the Home Team increases leverage of technology in its operations, how does the Home Team ensure its officers are adequately prepared and equipped to adapt to the rapid transformation?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In addition, I applaud the SPF's deployment of PolCams.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: At the same time, can I ask SPF for more PolCams to be deployed in congregation points across Boon Lay to better prevent and detect crimes?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In a 2019 global survey, it was found that Singaporean gamers spend more time playing electronic games than other Asian counterparts.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Loot boxes, a consumable virtual item used to redeem a randomised selection of further virtual items, is increasingly seen in some quarters as a form of gambling.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A study by academics at the University of York indicated that micro-transactions are rising as well.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In many games, these are to purchase loot boxes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Based on a Parliamentary Question I asked in January last year, the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) is studying the matter.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Belgium has banned loot boxes purchased using real money.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The United Kingdom's National Health Service has also called for the industry to ban loot boxes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Its Mental Health Director Claire Murdoch warned that these were in danger of "setting kids up for addiction".

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But now that crimes are more sophisticated and complex, it requires more mental dexterity and experience.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: At the same time, manpower constraints have gotten more severe with declining birth rates.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need a larger, better-equipped and skilled Home Team to deal with the challenges of today and tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Therefore, it is timely we extend the retirement and re-employment age of our Police Officers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I have had the privilege of serving with them for 13 years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I still meet many of them even now.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They have adapted well to the changing enforcement landscape and equipped themselves with new skills.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Some of the senior ones have gone into mentorship roles.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They polish their craft and master it over time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Then, they guide younger officers to do even better.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Establishing a second career can be difficult and we should help our officers to tide over a difficult period upon retirement after they have invested most of their lives in the Police Force.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I understand the operational difficulties of a significant jump in retirement age.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Extending the retirement and re-employment age will not only allow the Home Team to retain talent to meet growing security challenges but also buttress our longer-term crime-fighting strategies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must also ensure that we continue to invest in technology to help our officers combat crimes more effectively.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can the Minister share how we have been using technology to mitigate against emerging threats and manpower challenges?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In Malay):   I watched Senior Parliamentary Secretary Amrin Amin's efforts to engage the Malay/Muslim community to spread the anti-drug message through the Dadah Itu Haram campaign.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This campaign brings a deeper understanding about the efforts by the Government and the community in the fight against drugs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I also see this campaign as a good opportunity to create awareness about the challenges faced by ex-addicts.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This can encourage efforts to help addicts recover, turn over a new leaf and give back to society.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It seems that many people are now aware of this campaign and understand the important messages that it wants to send.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Will other plans be implemented to build on the current efforts?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I have seen the efforts to reach out to the Malay/Muslim community through the Dadah Itu Haram campaign.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There is clearly great value in taking a targeted approach and doing a community-specific engagement.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: By understanding the values within the community, the messages in the outreach efforts can be made more nuanced and would, therefore, have more impact to the people within the community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, has the Ministry carried out an assessment on the effectiveness of the community-specific public engagement approach in raising awareness in curbing drug abuse?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Has such a targeted approach resulted in better outcomes, especially in relation to reducing the number of addicts within the specific community or curbing the negative effects of drugs in the community?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: If such efforts have been showing results, are there upcoming plans to increase community-specific public education programmes?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank the Ministry for the various outreach efforts on drug abuse and community involvements to protect our people from drug abuse and rehabilitate the offenders and help their families.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: Among these efforts are those targeted at the Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: Can MHA provide an update on the ongoing efforts to engage the Malay/Muslim community with regard to drug abuse and whether there are other programmes or initiatives in the pipeline?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Mr Chairman, I believe the issue of drug abuse among our youths in Singapore is an important matter for our Government to address.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The potential damage and detrimental effects that drug abusers cause themselves, their families and the wider Singaporean Community can be significant.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This has been the cornerstone of our drug abuse policy in Singapore and I believe that the majority of Singaporeans strongly support the Government’s tough stance against drug abuse over the years.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The recent statistics for 2019 released by the Central Narcotics Bureau (CNB), however, suggests that we continue to have a worrying trend in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This is especially so when it is about new and young drug abusers.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Drug abusers in the 20 to 29 age group continue to form the largest group of abusers in 2019.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: One of the reasons for this worrying trend could be because our youths are being influenced by misinformation, especially in relation to what some deem as "less harmful soft drugs".

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Because of this, some of our youths may then adopt a more liberal attitude towards the use of drugs.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I invite the Minister to share with this House further details of the Ministry's plans on changing the drug narrative that influences our youths and to reduce the number of youths involved in the consumption of drugs.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, this cut concerns the topic of drug abuse among our youths.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Over the last two years, this House has continually affirmed our nation's zero-tolerance effort approach towards drugs.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Together, this House has passed legislation making it an offence to knowingly or recklessly leave the drugs or drug utensils within easy access of a child.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Despite these efforts, Mr Chairman, legislation alone will not solve our drug problem.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Our young people would not even flinch from using a hashtag like "#420".

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In this context, I raise three questions about the Ministry's preventive drug education efforts.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Can MHA update this House on the progress of this programme?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Second, outside the use of social media campaigns, are there current programmes launched by CNB to discourage youth consumption of drugs effective in deglamorising the consumption of drug use?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: What evidence do we have of its effectiveness?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, what efforts are being undertaken by CNB to work with high-risk communities, like the lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer or questioning, intersex and asexual (LGBTQIA) community, to discourage drug use?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Christopher de Souza, you can take your four cuts together.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In order to keep up the fight against drugs, we should deter both its supply and demand.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This will enable the many who are following the global drug debate to have a clear and accurate understanding as to the immense destruction that drug trafficking causes to human beings, families and children.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This will also provide the rationale behind why we, in Parliament, take strong positions against drug trafficking in and through Singapore and the consumption of drugs on our shores.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: A number of countries have legalised the consumption of cannabis.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: An increasing number of cannabis abusers worldwide is concerning.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: What are the plans to keep Singapore free from the scourge of cannabis abuse, especially given the mental and physical ill-effects of cannabis use and its dangerous characteristic as a gateway to harder and more deadly drugs?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Syndicates and criminal outfits are concocting new psychoactive substances at a fast pace.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The substances are finding their way into markets around the region.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: CNB is staffed with dedicated and professional officers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It should be ahead of the game by detecting New Psychoactive Substances (NPSes) early.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Also, the regime under the Misuse of Drugs Act (MDA) should be quick enough to classify newly concocted NPSes as illegal, thereby adding an extra legal deterrent effect.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Would the Minister provide an update on how and whether this better calibration has reduced the inmates' risks of reoffending?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is important to remind ourselves of the policy underpinning MHA's efforts on this front.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Senior Minister Teo Chee Hian, in a written reply issued in 2012 to a Parliamentary Question, stated as follows: "Effective rehabilitation and successful reintegration of offenders back into society contribute to a safer Singapore".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is, however, not an easy objective to achieve.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the recent past, there have been several structural changes implemented by this House to allow for better rehabilitation and reintegration of offenders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I will name two: the widening of community sentencing options for offenders and the revamp of the Reformative Training regime.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also note that SPF has also implemented other measures, such as increasing access to counsellors, providing better opportunities for education and skills training, and imposing Mandatory Aftercare Scheme for ex-offenders assessed to have a higher risk of reoffending.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It has also leveraged technology to foster closer relations between inmates and their family members as part of the rehabilitation process, for example, by allowing inmates to correspond with their family members through the e-letters system.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is timely, therefore, to review how these important changes have contributed to the mission of lowering the recidivism rates amongst offenders, and identify what further steps can be taken, not just by MHA but the rest of society, to achieve the objective of making Singapore safer.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would be grateful for an update, please.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: SCDF is an integral part of our frontline response team whenever Singaporeans encounter emergency medical situations in their everyday lives.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Their job, to put it mildly, is to respond quickly anywhere in Singapore and try to save the lives of Singaporeans in trouble.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: In fact, we can all see the tremendous work they do day to day as we continue to battle the COVID-19 virus outbreak in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I must take time to put on record our heartfelt appreciation to them and our medical healthcare team for their dedication and sacrifice in this ongoing battle.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: As each year passed, the SCDF EMS team has to deal with progressively larger volumes of medical emergency situations every day.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: That means that almost one in every 10 calls is a non-emergency or a false alarm.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: As we can imagine, such calls require the SCDF team to deploy resources which could otherwise have been dispatched to genuine life-threatening emergency cases.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: This is part of their continuing efforts and constitutes a key strategy in bringing down the number of such calls.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I, therefore. invite the Minister to share with this House the long-term plans and strategies on how the Home Team intends to ensure that the genuine emergency cases are attended to promptly and efficiently, especially in light of the resource constraints that SCDF faces.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, the fines for illegal u-turns, while attracting zero demerit points, were raised from $70 to $100 while heavy vehicle drivers saw the composition sum for the same offence increased from $100 to $150.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In fact, there was an increase in the composition fines for all offences that attracted fines of up to 12 demerit points.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, many of the residents I see who are on the receiving end of these new fines admit to their offences and are usually contrite.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In most cases, there is no question of actual harm caused, because that would attract more severe penalties anyway.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Those most heavily affected by the higher fines are taxi and private hire car drivers, motorcycle couriers and the low-income who may not have the ability to pay up such a large sum of money at one go.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the appropriate case, I would like to request the Ministry to consider the option of offering an automatic instalment plan for comparatively minor offences that do not attract a custodial sentence on the condition that the offender undertakes not to commit a similar offence, failing which no instalment plan would be offered as of right.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This approach seeks to retain the deterrence and policy objective of higher fines.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some jurisdictions around the world even offer to halve a fine provided it is paid forthwith.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Such a proposal can be modified for better policy outcomes, for example, with a requirement for some retraining or refresher defensive driving courses.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For first-time offenders only, I hope the Ministry can consider such alternatives that achieve the objective of increased road safety awareness and deterrence on the one hand and reasonable consideration for the financial consequences on frequent – usually low-income – road users on the other.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, I would like to bring up the issue of spam SMSes from illegal moneylenders and sports betting syndicates.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am sure I am not alone in this House to have received such SMSes.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Back in September last year, I filed a Parliamentary Question to ask about the measures the agencies have taken to tackle this issue.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I applaud the multi-agency effort between the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) and SPF to counter spam SMSes.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, these syndicates are finding other ways to bypass our measures.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some have used overseas numbers to send WhatsApp messages containing local numbers to contact.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There are also spam SMSes which are able to be sent out with their numbers masked, which made it more difficult to report or block such numbers.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The official advice is for anyone receiving such spam SMSes to report to SPF, either by a dedicated hotline or the i-Witness platform.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I have looked at the platform online and I find it to be rather tedious and this may discourage reporting.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Members of the public who receive such spam SMSes should be able to report simply by submitting a screenshot of the spam SMS directly to a designated number operated by IMDA and SPF.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With more people reporting, I hope we would be in a better position to close down these syndicates.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Mr Chairman, 2019 saw an increasing trend in the number of people falling prey to scams.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: The methods used by scammers range from e-commerce, loan, credit-for-sex, social media impersonation, Internet love scams, to investment scams.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: Scammers have even exploited the COVID-19 situation and impersonated Government agents conducting contact tracing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: The most recent scam is the fake email impersonation of President Halimah’s invitation for a dinner event with her, the Prime Minister and members of the Cabinet.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: While the elderly may be the target, a recent report indicates that six out of 10 persons who fall prey to scams in Singapore are persons aged 20-40.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: With high online usage in Singapore, it is not a surprise that online scams are increasing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: What is the Home Team's strategy to protect Singaporeans and to mitigate the prevalence of these scams?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The overall crime rate increased slightly last year mainly because of an increase in scams.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This seems to be the trend for the past few years.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The Home Team has put in a lot of effort over the years to educate the public, including having anti-scam programmes for the elderly and "Scamalert".

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: However, psychologically vulnerable people, regardless of age and background, continue to fall prey to scams, and scammers are evolving to become more sophisticated.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: What is the Home Team’s strategy to mitigate the prevalence of scams?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Besides online "love" scams and online shopping scams, concerns have been raised regarding the solicitation of donations through false representations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Such perpetrators tug on and exploit people’s altruistic intentions and then to rob them.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In such situations, instead of leaving the victim to pursue civil recourse in the Courts, would it not be better to charge the perpetrator – assuming he can be identified – in Court under section 420 of the Penal Code, that is, for cheating?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This would show that the state is taking the scams seriously.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In February 2020, two persons were sentenced to five and a half years' imprisonment for, amongst others, labour trafficking under the Prevention of Human Trafficking Act.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Will the Minister share what can be done to tighten detection of potential human trafficking cases across the different types of trafficking, for example, labour and sex trafficking?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: How is Singapore working with enforcement agencies overseas to track and punish cross-border illicit trafficking syndicates?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Harassment at the hands of runners belonging to unlicensed moneylending syndicates is mentally and physically draining.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The number of harassment cases related to unlicensed moneylending increased by 15% from 2018 to 2019.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The majority of these cases were via electronic means but nonetheless harrowing.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: What are the plans of the Home Team to deter and reduce the incidences of such harassment?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The impact can leave negative ill-effects or positive and lasting consequences of unity and common mission.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: During this COVID-19 crisis, how does the Home Team plan to garner community and public support in crisis preparedness and coordination such that Singapore society becomes stronger in the aftermath of a crisis?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Since we launched the SG Secure movement, can MHA share the progress of its outreach efforts, in particular, in the community as well as at workplaces?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I urge MHA to work with the community and businesses to recruit SG Secure Ambassadors at every HDB block and at every workplace.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: These ambassadors can help spread the SG Secure message and be equipped with first aid, automated external defibrillator (AED) and cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) skills.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: This is so that in the event of a terrorist attack and, especially the day after, these ambassadors can also help to handle the community or workplace response, as well as to ensure that the community is able to deal with emerging threats to safety and security.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: In fact, although SG Secure aims to prepare for major contingencies, it has been helpful and useful for grassroots volunteers, community partners and stakeholders, including residents, to prepare for major incidents, just like the fire incident in Boon Lay which happened last year which confronted myself and my community.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Mr Chairman, the Home Team has continued to do well in keeping Singapore as a safe and secure home.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: As Mr Teo Ser Luck mentioned earlier, if we look at the international rankings, Singapore has been doing well and it is something we see not just in the rankings but also in the lived experience of our communities.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Sometimes, on late-night walkabouts in Clementi town, which I help look after, I meet residents from different backgrounds and walks of life out and about at night on jalan-jalan, comfortable that even at night, it is alright to go out and walk around.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But this effort to keep Singapore safe is never-ending.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: As the world changes, criminals have found new ways to reach into our communities and heartlands to reach into the lives and minds of our people.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Today, I will speak on three challenges that the Home Team can hopefully continue to address even more in-depth and to a greater extent than before – terrorism, scams and drugs.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: On terrorism, Mr Chairman, Singapore has not experienced a terror attack in the past few years.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But we must never take this for granted.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Terrorism is a continuing threat to Singapore, as the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) continues to attract many followers with their violent ideology.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But it would be difficult, if not impossible, for MHA to fight terrorism alone.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Potential threats may go undetected if the general population is not aware, not alert and not on the lookout.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, it is critical to engage our community and build awareness.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Our entire nation and society are the frontlines against terrorism and, our defence, likewise, must be whole-of-society, whole-of-community, whole-of-nation.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, can the Minister share with us how will MHA be engaging the community at large to ensure that Singapore is well-prepared against the terrorism threat?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Social media has created new ways for people to keep in touch, whether from halfway around the world or from halfway across our island.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But it has also become a new channel for crime.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Based on a report by Consumers International, the widespread use of social media has brought new opportunities for criminals to connect with consumers and commit fraud, and scammers devising new and more innovative ways to trick people out of their money or harvest their personal data.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Scams have the potential to cause great harm to consumers, and the financial losses can be potentially life-changing.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: When a scammer succeeds, people can lose an entire lifetime's worth of savings.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And with electronic cash transfers, the misappropriated money can be in a different country within minutes of the scam, even before the victim has informed the authorities.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This is a global problem and many of us know of fellow Singaporeans who have been affected, too.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In 2019, Police statistics show that the total number of reported crimes increased by 6.3%, primarily due to a significant increase in scam cases.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, it is a worrying situation because, with each scam incident, someone has been deceived and lost his/her savings or harmed.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I understand that MHA has been working hard to address this issue.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In 2019, the Police set up the Anti-Scam Centre focusing on disrupting scammers’ operations and mitigating the monetary losses of victims by collaborating with financial institutions, telecommunication companies and digital platform owners.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But I am sure more can be done.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Furthermore, while the Police can work with institutions to deal with the situation, we must always remember that education is key, all the more so today because when scammers can reach out to people or our loved ones through mobile phones and instant messages, the additional safeguard of an informed and vigilant individual becomes more important than ever.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, the community needs to be made more aware of scams to avoid falling prey to scammers and prevent loved ones from being tricked and misled as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, can the Minister share with us how is MHA going to engage the community to help counter the increased threat of scams in our society?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Mr Chairman, on drug abuse, as a Member of Parliament looking after a constituency, as someone who has practised as a doctor, I have seen first-hand the damage that drugs can cause to families, patients, adults and the young.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Drug addiction exacts huge costs on the society – the costs of crime, of lives poisoned and destroyed, the costs that sometimes cannot be measured in dollars and cents alone.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But again, the cost is not just about dollars and cents.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is a human cost, a cost in our people's lives.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I understand that there was a local study on intergenerational offending.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is found that one in five inmates who are drug-abusing parents had children who had also committed crimes.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The researches assessed that this was due to the exposure to similar risk factors and adverse childhood experiences.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is a cost that can affect and can devastate a family across more than one generation.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It tells us that when drugs poison a family, it can poison not just the current generation, but affect the prospects of the next.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The poison of drugs can contribute to avoidable, adverse outcomes.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The poison of drugs can exacerbate inequality in a society.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our primary mission is to keep Singapore safe and secure, a safe and secure home.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If Members look at international rankings, as well as, more importantly, how our own people feel about their safety and security within Singapore, we do well.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our drug situation, something that I have spoken about quite frequently, Members have raised the point a number of times as well.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is not something that you would ever say you won the fight.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But the global situation, unfortunately, is getting worse with different regimes, a greater acceptance, a change in the legal position as well, where people are moving towards legalising in more and more countries, because they have lost the fight.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Whereas in Singapore, almost uniquely, we have managed to hold our own within the country.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If you look at fire safety, we again ranked first in the 2019 World Fires Statistics, for the second year running.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Moving on to our legislative calendar last year, I will touch on a couple of major aspects where we made legislative changes.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, we focused quite a bit on vulnerable victims and how we can protect them.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, the Penal Code was amended to cover more groups of vulnerable people, give them more protection, and enhance the deterrence.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Protection from Harassment Act (POHA) was also amended.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It allows victims of serious abuse who are in intimate relationships to get Protection Orders.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In the past, only married women could get such Protection Orders under the Women's Charter and others had to rely on normal rules on criminal law assault.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But we have given greater protection for those who are deemed to be in intimate partner relationships.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And if the perpetrator continues the harassment in breach of the Protection Orders, now, arrest is also possible.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And the processes have been simplified so that victims can seek Protection Orders quickly.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have previously more than once commended the good work done by Promoting Alternatives to Violence (PAVE) and organisations like PAVE.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They provide legal and other counselling services to such victims, victims of family violence, who could be victims of intimate partner violence or who could be victims in a marriage situation or in a marital situation.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Often, the individuals – I think Members would have come across them – feel unable to leave the relationship.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, they need a lot of help, they need a lot of counselling.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: A number of non-government organisations are involved in it, including, as I said, PAVE, to really take the steps that are needed to turn their lives around.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In fact, PAVE's advocacy played a crucial role in informing and shaping the POHA amendments.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They invited me to their Centre and shared with me what their clients go through.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As I said, this was August 2018, and I told them we will do something.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That really formed the basis of the amendments which we put through last year.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, it is a very good example of how civil society and the Government can work together to make real change on the ground.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The second key area that we worked on last year was in dealing with preventing clashes from religious differences.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These could be inter-religious as well as intra-religious.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our peace, progress and prosperity are all based on the social harmony that we have managed to foster in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And Members will know, worldwide, countries are struggling with identity politics and the fractured relationships between communities, and within communities in their respective countries.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our approach over the years, surveys, soundings and I think Members' own interactions with the residents show that people overwhelmingly support the approach we have taken to emphasise on harmony, and to come down quite hard on people who try and use religion as a basis to create public and social discord.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, people overwhelmingly support our stand against divisive rhetoric, against using religion for political ends.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And we have had the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act (MRHA) now for 29 years, as of last year.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: When it was first introduced, there was some disquiet.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And in a way, this framework actually has enhanced religious freedom within Singapore, because people of all religions – whatever your religious persuasion – feel confident, comfortable to go out there and practise their faiths.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And if you are agnostic, it is also the same.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, no one needs to feel uncomfortable in Singapore, because they know that there is a very protective framework that protects the freedom of religion.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And that confidence is based on the fact that the authorities both have the power to take effective action and will take effective and swift action on threats against religious harmony.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Among the amendments, we looked at our religious organisations.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We do not want them to become channels or conduits for foreigners to channel their own agenda into Singapore or impose their values.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We also put in various provisions to reduce conflicts, as I said not just among religions, but also within religion, intra-religion.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Also we do not want religion to be used as a basis for attacking other groups who may not be of a religious persuasion.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, say the lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender (LGBT) community.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: During engagements with the LGBT groups, many of them have told us they felt targeted as a community.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They should deal with their lives as they wish, but not use social or religious causes to attack one another.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That comes from the position that every Singaporean has his/her place in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They must feel safe and we will take actions against anyone who threatens anyone else's physical safety.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That was a brief survey on our international rankings, our approach and the legislative changes.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I earlier spoke about how our people, Singaporeans, feel about the Home Team.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Teo Ser Luck spoke about the importance of maintaining public trust and effectiveness in the Home Team.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That, to me, is fundamental, it is crucial.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Ninety percent trusts Home Team officers to do their duties objectively and with integrity.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In an SCDF survey, 99% were confident in SCDF's ability to cope with emergencies.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In an SPF survey, 90% trust the SPF as an organisation and they all agree that the Police Force is well-respected in the community.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And this trust is reflected in people's lived reality.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is more than any other place in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And if you were to look at the global average, that is 69%.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Parents are confident in letting their young children take public transport home alone, or anywhere alone.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These freedoms are priceless – the freedom to be yourself, the freedom to let your children be children, the freedom to know that they can grow up safe and secure.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These freedoms are priceless and they have come about because of our practical approach, our tough legal framework where we come down hard on offenders, and the fact that, within that framework, a broad level of freedom for people to carry on with their lives exists.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our people also trust the Home Team to manage incidents effectively.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In our surveys, 89% of respondents are confident in the Home Team's ability to manage national crises.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Talking about national crises, of course, we are dealing with COVID-19 now.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked how have the Home Team officers been deployed in the national fight against the virus.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Members would have seen from newspaper reports that Home Team officers, together with others from the agencies involved, have been working round the clock in dealing with COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Many of the officers are at the frontlines.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If you look at the border control and health screening measures, at the checkpoints with hundreds of thousands of people coming in every day.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Officers are also securing Government Quarantine Facilities and checking on persons under quarantine; supporting, quite crucially, the Ministry of Health's (MOH's) contact-tracing operations.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Criminal Investigation Department (CID) has lent its expertise, a team of officers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Their work has been reported fairly extensively and they have done quite exceptional work.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The kind of contact-tracing that has been done is very detailed.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I do not think you see a parallel anywhere else in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Home Team officers have also helped to conduct swabbing operations among suspect cases, which puts them on the frontline.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And for the second planeload of Singaporeans that the Government flew back from Wuhan and also, of course, our officers helped convey suspect cases to hospital.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: MHA is part of the multi-Ministry task force involved in the whole-of-Government response to the crisis.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: All of that, of course, comes on top of the officers' day-to-day responsibilities, which have to carry on.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have to say I join many Singaporeans, and I am sure I join Members of Parliament, in saying that we are very proud of the way all our public officers have responded, including, if I may say, Home Team officers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Members will know that the Home Team, the Police Force and the rest of the Home Team, are actually very lean, like much of the Public Service.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, much leaner compared to any of these cities, but our outcomes are much better compared with any of them.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And I think it comes from a combination of many years of a proper law and order framework, which went against international opinions sometimes.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The fact that if you have committed a crime in Singapore, you are going to be prosecuted regardless of who you are.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And if you are guilty or likely to be found guilty, and cases do not stretch for years and years, and punishment is, therefore, reasonably certain.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These factors and the whole attitude that is supportive of our law and order framework, amongst a vast majority of our population, have meant that people who want to break the laws are a very small minority.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That has allowed our taxpayer funds to be put to other uses and not the heavy policing that you see in many other countries.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Yet, we still give the outcomes that people want in terms of safety and security, and how they feel about the country.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza and Miss Cheng Li Hui asked how the Home Team can remain effective and operational in a changing environment.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That requires continued heavy investments into the capabilities of the officers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We work with our partners to encourage our officers to engage in continuous learning and upskilling, just like the rest of society, from recruitment to retirement.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That will allow us to tap on the experience of our more mature officers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It will enhance career transition efforts and it will help them secure a meaningful second career after retiring from the Home Team.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This year is a very important year for SPF.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is the SPF200, as many Members would know.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I am told that it was the first, if not, the second organisation that was set up in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If you go back to colonial times, understandably the British may have set up the Customs first before they set up the Police Force.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Subject to that, in the 200 years, we have seen the Home Team grow from strength to strength.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Miss Cheng Li Hui and Mr Christopher de Souza remarked about SPF's 200 years.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If Members go back to the early 19th century, we were a booming town but a booming immigrant town with more than its fair share of social ills – lawlessness, rampant piracy, clandestine activities among secret societies, riots among the different Chinese dialect groups.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And there was really an urgent need for law and order.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: By 1846, the first set of rules and regulations was established and they spelt out the duties, the way Police Officers conduct themselves.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: When we move to a century later, in the 1900s, the Criminal Procedure Code and Criminal Registry Department were set up, and a fingerprint system was also set up and new Police buildings were constructed.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Fast forward to after the Second World War, the "999" hotline was established and the Radio Division was established.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Then, after the Maria Hertogh riots, the Riot Squad was set up.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: After 1965, Independence, the Police have taken on an even greater role in the safety and security of our society.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Police National Service was introduced in 1967 and the first Neighbourhood Police Post in 1983.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That really transformed the image of the Police Officer, not just as a person enforcing the law but also as a member of the community, out there in the community, helping people and responding to incidents.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Then, we had the 11 September incidents in New York which changed the operating landscape yet again, a new normal.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We had to build counter-terrorism capabilities and put in place safety measures.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I would say that after the 2015 attacks in Paris, yet again, we had to step up considerably to look at the fact that a variety of soft targets could be attacked by terrorists.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, Members will agree with me, today, if we look at SPF, it is a highly capable professional Police Force and highly-regarded.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And our SPF officers deserve our recognition and appreciation for their professionalism, their readiness and sacrifice over the years.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And we will also get additional boats and that would be a significant upgrade to PCG's abilities to handle such incidents.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I am confident that the Police Force, as a whole, will continue to uphold the tradition of excellence so that Singaporeans will continue to enjoy the very high levels of safety, security, law and order.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Safety and security are not just the responsibility of law enforcers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I want to move away from the usual COS speech to say something a little bit more philosophical, maybe even reflective.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And this comes from some of the points made by Members of Parliament, including Mr Christopher de Souza, who questioned about the street protests that have taken place around the world.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think it comes back to this point: you can have the best police force in the world but you cannot deal with riots unless there are other things that are taken care of as well.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have had riots across the world, in Chile, Europe, Hong Kong, of course, and other places.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They have disrupted the lives of ordinary citizens and destroyed public and private infrastructure.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have had in Lebanon, where several months of protests have caused a lot of damage.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Santiago, I mentioned, demonstrators were enraged by hikes in public transport fares.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They looted stores and set fires to vehicles and properties.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Then we saw Hong Kong, seven months of protest.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked what can we learn from these protests.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will take this opportunity to discuss Hong Kong and the others and what are the lessons for us.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have seen hundreds of thousands of people on the streets in Hong Kong.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Some of them have engaged in extremely violent, disruptive behaviour, with the whole purpose of crippling the government and inflicting severe damage to the economy and to the reputation of the city, and obviously caused very severe challenges for the Hong Kong Police Force.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Before this latest period of unrest, the Hong Kong Police Force was considered one of the finest in Asia.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That, I would say, has severely damaged the relationship between the police and the public – not helped by the one-sided portrayal of the situation in the media.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In particular, the international media often focused on criticising only the police force.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As for the police, there was always reference to their brutality and their alleged brutal response.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The first time a police officer fired a live round, the media depicted it as an example of police brutality, and the picture went round the world.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But all the events leading up to that point were ignored.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Protestors, as I said, were often portrayed in a positive light.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That the police were being attacked, their lives were frequently in danger, their families were being exposed – all that was ignored.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The protestors were not just violent towards the police.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Hong Kong residents who went to try and clean up were set upon by the protestors.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In one instance, a man was hit over the head with a drain cover by masked assailants while clearing the roadblocks.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Today, just before the COVID-19 situation, the Hong Kong police force were seriously stretched.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They faced persistent criticism both domestically and internationally.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Some countries that have traditionally said, "The freedom to protest is part of the freedom of expression and should not be clamped down".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But, you know, when it comes to the crunch, they take different steps.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, in 2009, Copenhagen hosted a United Nations (UN) climate conference.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Chairman, with your permission, may I display a slide on the LCD screen?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Anyone who protested would find themselves in there.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In London, climate activists calling themselves the Extinction Rebellion mounted non-violent protests for two weeks last year.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They conducted marches, blockaded roads and disrupted train services.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In one protest, an activist climbed onto the roof of a train during the morning rush hour.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They dragged him off the roof and assaulted him.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the Metropolitan Police then banned the Extinction Rebellion protests across London.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have been criticised for disallowing protests outside of Speaker’s Corner, even if it was with just one person.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How do we tell what will be a peaceful protest and what will escalate into violence?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Part of the issue in Hong Kong is that protests are allowed, the police are only allowed to intervene when it turns violent.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, by the time you have 50,000 people on the streets and some people go in there, let us say 500, mixed up, who are deliberately intent on creating violence, how do the police handle this?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Sometimes, people want to protest, say, take iconic places – Orchard Road or Tanglin or places like that – where there is a lot of commercial activity, primarily because of the disturbance it would cause to everyone else and, therefore, their cause would get noticed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, on the one side is the desire of the protestors to get themselves noticed, on the other side is the disamenity to the rest of the community.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why should protests be favoured and why should the rest of the community say just accept it?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why not we put a place, if you want to protest, you go to a specified place and you protest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Otherwise, the best police force in the world would still not be able to handle it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The second is that it cannot be seen purely as a law and order issue.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you seek to deal with protests and your approach to protests is simply to have tough laws and enforce them, it is not going to work.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because underlying it is what is your social order, what is the level of inequality, what is the social justice, how do people feel in your society?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Do they, by and large, believe that they benefit from the system?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why should they support a system that is fundamentally unfair?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Those who are familiar with Chinese history will understand legalism, going back to the Qin dynasty, during the Warring States period.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That was the preferred way of bringing order to a chaotic, fractious society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The emperor’s rule was based on strict laws, harsh enforcement and collective punishments.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But such a system cannot carry on for long.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: People often misunderstand and think that our approach is based on very strict punishments.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Now, it is, first and foremost, based on making sure that the majority progresses, and that the system is fair.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Strict punishments can only be built on such a system.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Qin emperor's rule, as people will note, collapsed because the approach actually worsened people's social and economic lives.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: China’s emperors tried to follow Confucianism, which depended solely or primarily on the leaders setting the example and inspiring people to be like them, family and social harmony, a responsible government with the moral duty to promote harmony.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Confucianism appealed to people because they enjoyed internal peace and stability, and under it, the country experienced remarkable progress.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it had limitations as well because in every society, a large majority of people can be inspired to be good, to be noble, to do the right thing, following the example of leaders, assuming you have leaders who can inspire that kind of confidence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But you will always have a group that will want to challenge your laws, that will want to break them and that will want to destabilise.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You will need to deal with them through a system of laws which can be enforced.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What framework, how strict, what you allow, what you do not allow must be for each society to decide.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, you have to build the society on the basis of fairness, upholding moral responsibility on the part of the leadership, proper governance, an approach of upright virtuous governance which inspires people and bring that across to the people as a whole and then deal with the law breakers in a way that makes it clear to everybody that the laws would be applied, fairly, evenly, and law-breaking will be dealt with.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If there is good governance and people benefit, you can always deal with a small number who want to disrupt.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: With that background, let me deal with the specific question that Mr Pritam Singh asked.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think all of us agree, including Mr Pritam Singh, that there can be very significant social costs through irresponsible driving.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Yes, in specific cases, there may be no incidents, no loss of life.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But imagine when there is loss of life.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You lose your three-year-old child or you lose your grandmother or grandfather through somebody else's irresponsible driving.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And, unfortunately, over the last few years, we have seen an increase or enough incidents of people driving when they should not be driving, when they were under suspension, or driving when they are under the influence of alcohol.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: People have died as a result of those actions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we want to send, I wanted to send a very strong signal that penalties are going to be enhanced because we cannot accept people being irresponsible on the roads.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I made a speech saying that we are going to now deal with this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It arose from an incident where a young man who was under suspension drove and hit someone and killed him, if my memory serves me right, a lorry driver.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In that case, the young man was from a higher socio-economic group.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The lorry driver was from the lower socio-economic group.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If they have accumulated up to one third of the maximum points, if they go for the Safe Driving Course, then, their accumulated points would be taken out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
